lines: Here's the big idea, friend. Jesus tells a story about a manager the text flat-out calls dishonest (Luke 16:8), and He uses it to teach His disciples about money. Money runs out, so use it with the end in view, and don't ever let it be your master (Luke 16:1-13).

What gets praised is NOT his honesty. The master commends him because he had acted shrewdly (Luke 16:8). He saw the end coming and got ready for it (Luke 16:4). Then the line right after says, "the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light." (Luke 16:8) Baker, that's your coworker with a five-year plan, while I'm over here still looking for my other oven mitt.

So Jesus says to use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves, so that "when it is gone," they will welcome you into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9). WHEN it is gone. Not if. Money runs out. So spend the stuff that runs out on the stuff that lasts forever.

And no, Jesus is not handing out gold stars for creative math. He says whoever is dishonest with very little will also be dishonest with much (Luke 16:10). Then He asks it straight: if you haven't been faithful with worldly wealth, who will entrust you with true riches (Luke 16:11)?

Friend, how you handle the little stuff, even stuff that belongs to somebody else, shows what you'd do with the big stuff (Luke 16:10-12). Think about it. If I sneak cookies out of a box I'm holding for you, you are NOT handing me the keys to your bakery.

Then Jesus lands it: "You cannot serve both God and money." (Luke 16:13) Money can be a tool in your hand. It cannot be the boss of your heart. One master. This is NOT a job share. And Jesus isn't done talking about money yet.
